reasoning: The code claim is accurate. ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:91 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:128 read files with Data(contentsOf:options:[.mappedIfSafe]). The only guards before the read are a size/mtime memo lookup (ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:77-88) and a Task.isCancelled check (:65). Neither stops a file from being truncated after it is mapped. So nothing in the code protects the mapped bytes. That does not make this a vulnerability, because the attack never crosses a trust boundary. The finding's own precondition is write access to ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex/sessions. Those directories are owned by the same macOS user who runs the menu-bar app. The operating system's per-user isolation is the defense, and it holds: another user, a sandboxed process or a remote party cannot write there. A same-user process that can write there already has a strictly stronger way to cause the claimed harm. It can send kill -9 to the app, delete or edit its config, or change the credential files the app reads. The only claimed impact is a crash that repeats (denial of service). This path gives the attacker nothing they did not already have, so there is no mitigation missing across a boundary. Switching to a plain read would be a sensible robustness fix against a CLI truncating its own files, but that is a reliability issue, not a security finding.
